Here are **well-known British poems that are firmly in the public domain** (authors died more than 70 years ago). I’ve grouped them so you can quickly see what might suit your purpose.

---

## Medieval & Early English
- **“Beowulf”** (anonymous, c. 8th–11th century)  
- **“Sir Gawain and the Green Knight”** (anonymous, 14th century)  
- **Geoffrey Chaucer**
  - *The Canterbury Tales* (incl. “The General Prologue”)

---

## Renaissance & Elizabethan
- **William Shakespeare**
  - Sonnets (e.g. Sonnet 18: *“Shall I compare thee to a summer’s day?”*)
  - Narrative poems (*Venus and Adonis*, *The Rape of Lucrece*)
- **Sir Philip Sidney**
  - Sonnets from *Astrophel and Stella*
- **Christopher Marlowe**
  - *“The Passionate Shepherd to His Love”*

---

## Metaphysical Poets (17th century)
- **John Donne**
  - *“No Man Is an Island”*
  - *“The Flea”*
  - *“A Valediction: Forbidding Mourning”*
- **George Herbert**
  - *“Love (III)”*
- **Andrew Marvell**
  - *“To His Coy Mistress”*

---

## Romantic Poets
- **William Blake**
  - *“The Tyger”*
  - *“London”*
  - *Songs of Innocence and of Experience*
- **William Wordsworth**
  - *“I Wandered Lonely as a Cloud”*
  - *“Tintern Abbey”*
- **Samuel Taylor Coleridge**
  - *“Kubla Khan”*
  - *“The Rime of the Ancient Mariner”*
- **Lord Byron**
  - *“She Walks in Beauty”*
- **Percy Bysshe Shelley**
  - *“Ozymandias”*
  - *“Ode to the West Wind”*
- **John Keats**
  - *“Ode to a Nightingale”*
  - *“Ode on a Grecian Urn”*

---

## Victorian Poets
- **Alfred, Lord Tennyson**
  - *“Ulysses”*
  - *“In Memoriam A.H.H.”*
- **Robert Browning**
  - *“My Last Duchess”*
- **Elizabeth Barrett Browning**
  - Sonnets from *Sonnets from the Portuguese*
- **Christina Rossetti**
  - *“Remember”*
  - *“Goblin Market”*
- **Matthew Arnold**
  - *“Dover Beach”*

---

## Late 19th / Early 20th (Still Public Domain)
- **A. E. Housman**
  - Poems from *A Shropshire Lad*
- **Thomas Hardy**
  - *“The Darkling Thrush”*
- **Rudyard Kipling**
  - *“If—”*
  - *“Recessional”*

---

entries.title: The genius of Seamus Heaney (plus Swallow, an exclusive new poem)
entries.snippet:
This article commemorates the life and legacy of Nobel laureate Seamus Heaney, highlighting the comprehensive new volume The Poems of Seamus Heaney published by Faber. Spanning nearly 1,300 pages, the collection gathers his poetic work, commentary, and 25 previously unpublished poems curated by Heaney's family. The piece traces Heaney’s journey from his rural roots in Bellaghy, Northern Ireland, to international literary acclaim, examining signature works like "Digging," "Death of a Naturalist," and "North" as well as his responses to The Troubles.

The article includes reflections from loved ones and collaborators, including his brother Dan Heaney and editor Bernard O'Donoghue, underscoring Heaney’s humility, approachability, and deep local ties. It also explores the controversies surrounding his poem “Punishment,” delving into feminist critiques and Heaney’s engagement with ethical complexity. Poet Susannah Dickey attests to his lasting influence on contemporary verse.

The article concludes with a newly uncovered poem, “Swallow,” written in 2010, illustrating Heaney’s enduring poetic sensibility and introspective voice. It reaffirms his ability to find profound meaning in small details, anchoring his global impact in a deeply personal and local perspective.

Simon Armitage releases spring-themed poetry collection celebrating blossom
entries.snippet:
Poet Laureate Simon Armitage has released a new spring-themed poetry collection, *Blossomise*, in collaboration with the National Trust to celebrate World Poetry Day and the arrival of spring. The collection, inspired by a year of visiting blossom sites across the UK—including gardens, rural areas, parks, and urban centers—reflects on the beauty and symbolism of blossom while addressing contemporary issues like climate change. Armitage describes blossom as a metaphorical artist and weathervane, representing both joy and environmental fragility.

The collection includes more than the intended ten poems, with eleven haiku added as a nod to Japanese literary traditions. Accompanying the release is an EP by Armitage’s band, LYR, featuring five song adaptations of the poems, produced collaboratively with community choirs and student filmmakers. Performances are planned at various blossom sites from Plymouth to Newcastle to coincide with the northward progression of spring.

Illustrated by Angela Harding, *Blossomise* is part of the National Trust’s ongoing blossom campaign, originally launched during the COVID-19 lockdown. The campaign encourages the public to embrace the seasonal beauty through reading, music, and outdoor experiences tied to the blooming spectacle.

entries.title: Iris Murdoch's poems on bisexuality to be published - read one exclusively here
entries.snippet:
A new poetry collection by acclaimed novelist and philosopher Iris Murdoch, titled *Poems from an Attic: Selected Poems, 1936–1995*, is set for release on November 6, 2025. This publication marks the first time Murdoch’s bisexuality is openly explored in her creative work, offering a more intimate understanding of her personal relationships and inner life. The anthology, comprising 88 previously unpublished or little-known poems, spans nearly six decades and was compiled from notebooks discovered in the attic of her Oxford home in 2016.

Known primarily for her philosophical novels, including the Booker Prize-winning *The Sea, The Sea*, Murdoch also wrote poetry throughout her life, remaining largely private about it. The collection explores themes such as love, heartbreak, friendship, and sexual fluidity, with notable pieces like “The dear and detailed dream of your carved head,” believed to reflect her relationship with philosopher Elizabeth Anscombe. Editor Sarah Hall praises Murdoch’s nuanced engagement with issues of sexuality and emotional vulnerability, presenting her as intellectually bold and emotionally daring. The volume offers a poignant, autobiographical glimpse into one of the 20th century's most revered literary minds.

Here’s a helpful guide to **British poems in the public domain** — especially classics you can read freely. (Most *very recent* British poetry is **not yet** in the public domain, since UK copyright generally lasts until **70 years after the author’s death** — so poets who died after ~1955 aren’t public domain yet.)

---

## 📜 What *is* Public Domain Poetry?

Public domain poems can be used, shared, and reproduced without permission because the copyright has expired (typically 70 years after the author’s death in the UK).

Most British poems in the public domain are by authors who died before 1955 (e.g., Victorian, Georgian, and early 20th-century writers).

---

## 📚 Classic British Poems in the Public Domain

Here are examples of well-known public domain works by British poets:

### **William Blake (1757–1827)**
- **“The Tyger”** — one of his most famous poems, from *Songs of Experience*. citeturn0search3

### **Lord Byron (1788–1824)**
- **“She Walks in Beauty”** — a popular lyrical poem celebrating beauty and calm. citeturn0search6

### **Robert Browning (1812–1889)**
- **Various dramatic monologues and lyrics**, widely available in public domain collections. citeturn0search1

### **John Donne (1572–1631)**
- **“Death, be not proud”** (Holy Sonnet X) — a renowned metaphysical poem. citeturn0search8

### **Robert Louis Stevenson (1850–1894)**
- Children’s favorites like **“My Shadow”** and **“Bed in Summer”**. citeturn0search3

### **Christina Rossetti (1830–1894)**
- **“Who Has Seen the Wind?”** — short and evocative, public domain work. citeturn0search3

### **Thomas Hardy (1840–1928)**
- Poems like **“The Convergence of the Twain”**, about the sinking of the *Titanic*. citeturn0search3

### **Rudyard Kipling (1865–1936)**
- Many of his poems (e.g., **“The Mary Gloster”**) are in the public domain because he died before the copyright cutoff. citeturn0search48

### **John Masefield (1878–1967)**
- Masefield’s early work is in the public domain (later poems may still be copyrighted). citeturn0search22

---

## 📘 Where to Find British Public Domain Poetry Online

You can explore large collections of public domain works here:

- **Public-Domain Poetry (indexed site)** — thousands of poems by historic authors. citeturn0search0  
- **Representative Poetry Online (University of Toronto)** — searchable archive including British poets across centuries. citeturn0search7  
- **Public Domain Review (poetry category)** — curated historic works and essays. citeturn0search5  
- **Wikisource Public Domain Poetry Collections** — searchable text of many older poems. citeturn0search20  

---

## ❗ About *Newest* British Public Domain Poetry

Currently, *very recent British poetry* (e.g., works published after mid-20th century or by poets who died less than 70 years ago) is **not yet in the public domain** in the UK.

For example:

- Modern British poets like **Simon Armitage** (alive) or **Carol Ann Duffy** (died 2024) are *not* in the public domain (Duffy’s works will enter public domain 70 years post-death). citeturn0search45

So “newest” in the public domain means works by authors who died before ~1955.

---

## 🧾 Examples of British Public Domain Poems You Can Access Now

Here are just a few *public domain* British poems you can look up by title:

1. **“The Tyger”** – William Blake citeturn0search3  
2. **“She Walks in Beauty”** – Lord Byron citeturn0search6  
3. **“Death, be not proud”** – John Donne citeturn0search8  
4. **“My Shadow”** – Robert Louis Stevenson citeturn0search3  
5. **“Who Has Seen the Wind?”** – Christina Rossetti citeturn0search3  
6. **“The Convergence of the Twain”** – Thomas Hardy citeturn0search3  
7. **Selected maritime poems by John Masefield** (public domain) citeturn0search22

If by **“most lyrical”** you mean poems that are **melodic, musical, emotionally flowing, and easy to set to music or read aloud**, these are widely regarded as the *most singable / lyrical* **British public-domain poems**:

---

## 🌿 Top-Tier Lyrical British Poems (Public Domain)

### ⭐ **William Blake**
Blake is *the* gold standard for lyricism.
- **“The Lamb”** – hymn-like, pure, simple rhythm  
- **“The Tyger”** – strong beat, chant-like intensity

Yes — that reaction makes complete sense.

**That’s exactly why *The Salutation* feels so striking today.**  
It comes from a mental world that is almost **absent** in a culture surrounded by accumulation, ownership, leverage, branding, optimisation.

Traherne isn’t saying *“I want”* or *“I take”*.  
He’s saying:

- *Everything already is*  
- *Nothing needs to be seized*  
- *Value precedes possession*

What feels unfamiliar now:

- **No competition** — nothing is scarce in the poem  
- **No anxiety** — no fear of missing out, no comparison  
- **No extraction** — the world is received, not exploited  
- **No performance** — joy exists without being displayed or monetised  

Even the repeated **“Are mine”** isn’t greedy.  
It’s almost the *opposite* of modern ownership.

Today, “mine” usually means:
- exclusion
- control
- advantage

For Traherne, “mine” means:
- participation
- belonging
- gratitude

That mindset is rare now — not because it’s naïve, but because it **doesn’t fit systems built on scarcity and pressure**.

So when you say it feels *interesting but unfamiliar*, that’s not distance —  
that’s recognition of something **we’ve lost touch with**.

- stay quietly with *why* this clashes with modern greed,
